newsitem.title: UK: Inflation no danger as UK producer prices hit new low.
newsitem.headline: Inflation no danger as UK producer prices hit new low.

text.p: British inflationary pressures eased off sharply in January as the price of goods leaving factory gates dropped to a 10-year low, according to official figures released on Monday.
Economists said the figures would help the Conservative government to avoid politically unpopular increases in interest rates before the looming election.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said output prices -- factory gate prices -- rose 0.2 percent in January and were up just 1.5 percent from a year earlier, the lowest rate of increase since October 1986.
Input prices, a measure of the cost of raw materials and fuel, fell 0.6 percent in January and were down 6.3 percent from a year earlier.
"The weather is set fair for our inflation outlook," Treasury minister Angela Knight said in a statement.

Economists said the figures would provide further ammunition for Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke to resist pressure from the Bank of England to raise interest rates to prevent a resurgence of inflation.
"I'm sure Kenneth Clarke is singing in his bath on these numbers -- they are very good indeed," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International in London.
The central bank has been urging an increase in interest rates from the present 6.0 percent since December.
But Clarke, who is anxious to avoid a move which would mean costlier home loans for millions of Britons, has so far refused, arguing that the economic picture is mixed.
An election must be held by May 22 and the ruling Conservatives are well behind the opposition Labour party in opinion polls.

Core output prices, which exclude food, drink, tobacco and petroleum and are seen by financial markets as a better indicator of inflation pressures, rose 0.6 percent in the year to January -- the lowest growth rate for almost 30 years.
Economists said a strong pound, which makes imports cheaper, and lower prices for some commodities would ensure input prices presented no threat to inflation for the time being.
"Today's figures are excellent and confirm once again that inflation pressures at the factory-gate level are minimal," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in London.
"Clarke may be forgiven a wry smile. His judgement, after all, appears more in tune with recent economic data."

The strength of sterling, which has gained around 14 percent on a trade-weighted basis since August last year, was a dominant factor in Monday's data, exerting strong downward pressure on industry costs.
Economists said this was likely to continue and would help Clarke to justify holding interest rates steady in the coming months, depite recent signs of a pick up in consumer spending.
The government's target is for underlying inflation of 2.5 percent, but falls in unemployment, triggering more enthusiastic consumer activity, held inflation at 3.1 percent last month.

While Monday's figures were unlikely to have a direct impact on high street prices, economists said continued weakness in producer prices would help offset any inflationary pressure from the consumer side.

"With so much good news further down the inflation pipeline, even a sharp rebound in retail margins as consumer spending strengthens will not prevent underlying inflation from falling sharply this year," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets in London.
